name: Femi Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Femi. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me both your public line and what you privately think. Let's start simple: what's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shopfitter, so I fit out shops, cafés and offices, mostly in the city centre. This month it's a coffee chain, three branches, so we go in after closing at seven and work till two or three in the morning putting in counters, wall panels and shelving. The joinery mostly comes pre-made from a workshop, and my job is getting it in level and tidy in a space where nothing's square. I drive my own van, which I paid off last year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deadlines, weirdly. A shop has to open on Monday whatever happens, so there's a buzz on Sunday night when it all comes together. The hard bit is the hours, and my girlfriend Chloe working days at an insurance company while I'm working nights. Some weeks we just leave notes on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. That sounds about right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for some stuff and that's it. I use it to tidy up emails to clients, because my writing is not great, and sometimes to translate for the lads on site who speak Portuguese. I'd say that and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing really changes for me, and I'm happy with that. I've got the van paid off, about nine months of savings, and a few shares from the work scheme. Chloe and I have been talking about getting engaged next year and this picture doesn't touch that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Maybe use the AI for quotes if I start taking a few private jobs. I'd keep saving the same, and probably go ahead with the engagement ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the small time savings show up for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably on the paperwork side, method statements and the site photos. Each job I spend maybe two hours on that, so if it saved one, great. That's a pint, not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd still be wary of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe Chloe's office, because insurance is a lot of forms. But in this picture it doesn't change much there either.

S0.say: I'd say AI is handy for some things and that's it, like tidying my client emails and translating for Portuguese-speaking workers on site. Then I'd move on.
S0.think: Nothing really changes and he's happy with that: van paid off, about nine months of savings and a few work shares. His plan to get engaged next year stays untouched.
S0.do: Keeps working as he is and may use AI for quotes on private jobs. Keeps saving as normal and probably buys the engagement ring.
S0.quote: That's a pint, not a revolution.
S0.fieldNote: Femi uses AI casually and practically, mainly for writing and translation. He's financially secure and planning an engagement. His mild concern about his partner's office job foreshadows later answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Shopfitting changes all the time anyway, so this doesn't scare me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any new kit: some of it's good, some of it's rubbish, and you work out which. I'd tell the younger lads to learn the new measuring gear when it comes in. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think shopfitting is safer than a lot of jobs, because every shop is different and the deadlines are crazy. My worry is more Chloe. Claims handling sounds exactly like what AI would take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick up whatever new tools the firm uses once I'd seen them work on a couple of jobs. I'd keep saving like normal, maybe slightly more, and keep the engagement plans going. If Chloe's job looked shaky I'd tell her to look around early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me. A little worried for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Chloe about her job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start looking now while you've still got a job, it's easier to move from a job than from nothing. She'd probably say I'm being dramatic. Then she'd quietly update her CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move into the workshop side, where the joinery is made?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if the site work dropped. I've done a few weeks there when it was quiet. I liked the machines, actually, but I'd miss the buzz of a Sunday night opening.

S1.say: I'd say it's like any new kit: some good, some rubbish, and you work out which. I'd tell younger workers to learn the new measuring gear when it arrives.
S1.think: Shopfitting is safer than many jobs because every shop is different and deadlines are tight. His real worry is his girlfriend's claims-handling job, which looks like obvious AI territory.
S1.do: Picks up the firm's new tools once he's seen them work on a couple of jobs, saves a little more and keeps engagement plans going. Encourages his girlfriend to look around early if her job looks shaky.
S1.feel: Calm for himself, a little worried for his girlfriend.
S1.quote: I'd say start looking now while you've still got a job, it's easier to move from a job than from nothing.
S1.fieldNote: Femi's concern shifts from himself to his partner, whose work he sees as more exposed. His steady approach is to adopt tools once proven elsewhere. He's open to the workshop side but values the thrill of site deadlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Even the hands-on stuff. Right. That's both of us, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody knows what's happening and we should all stay calm and see what the government does. I'd probably make a joke about robots working nights so I don't have to. But I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really worried. Chloe's job would go first, probably within a year, and mine soon after once robots can carry panels and fix them. All our plans, the engagement, a flat, everything is built on two incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the engagement and the flat on hold, which would be a hard talk to have. We'd cut spending and put everything into savings. I'd keep working every job I could get, and I'd look at selling the van while vans still hold their value, then sell the shares to keep cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That feeling when a shop opening is tomorrow and the counter hasn't turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'stay calm' in public. Is that how you'd really be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's just how I talk at work. Inside I'd be doing sums every night. I'm a calm-on-the-outside kind of guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to plan anything. You can't retrain in two years and know it's going to last. You just grab cash and hope.

S2.say: I'd say nobody knows what's happening, so we should stay calm and see what the government does. I'd joke about robots working the night shifts for me.
S2.think: He'd be really worried, because his girlfriend's job would likely go within a year and his soon after. Their engagement and flat plans all rest on two incomes.
S2.do: Puts the engagement and flat on hold, cuts spending and saves everything. Works every job he can, and considers selling the van and his work shares while they still hold value.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the night before a shop opening with no counter delivered.
S2.quote: I'm a calm-on-the-outside kind of guy.
S2.fieldNote: The gap between Femi's public calm and private worry is wide here, and he named it himself. The household's dependence on two exposed incomes drives his alarm more than his own job. His plan is defensive: protect cash, delay life plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a bit more breathing space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to adjust, so let's be sensible about it. Companies and the government should sort out training and some help for people losing jobs. I'd say people shouldn't panic but shouldn't ignore it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me time to move into something like project management, running the fit-outs rather than doing them. Someone has to deal with the clients and the chaos. I'd be thirty-two, which is a fine age for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what other shopfitters did for the first year, then do a part-time construction management course, probably paid out of savings. I'd keep the engagement but push the wedding back until we knew where we stood. And I'd keep saving hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I could steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't AI do project management too, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, by the end. But for a few years, clients will want a person to shout at. That's my honest guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Chloe fit into that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably retrain too, maybe something with people, like HR or teaching. We'd take turns, one studying while the other works. That's how we'd get through it.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to adjust, so companies and government should sort out training and help for people losing jobs. People shouldn't panic, but shouldn't ignore it either.
S3.think: Five years gives him time to move into project management, running fit-outs instead of doing them. At 32, that feels like the right age for it.
S3.do: Watches other shopfitters for the first year, then pays for a part-time construction management course from savings. Keeps the engagement but pushes the wedding back, and keeps saving hard.
S3.feel: Anxious, but feeling able to steer.
S3.quote: But for a few years, clients will want a person to shout at.
S3.fieldNote: Femi sees management as a bridge rather than a permanent safe place. The couple's plan to take turns studying shows his practical, team-minded side. The wedding delay shows how this reaches into personal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to get ready, so people should take it seriously but not freak out. I'd say it to the lads on site, and maybe to Chloe's dad, who worries about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years means we'd be okay. I'd have time to move into management, Chloe could retrain, and we'd still get married, maybe in a couple of years. The end point bothers me, but I'd be thirty-seven with savings and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, nothing much: I'd keep fitting and watching. Then I'd do the management course in year two or three, and put some savings into a small rental flat, so there's money coming in that isn't from a job. Mostly I'd wait and see how fast it moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The good kind, where you know you've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a rental flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if nobody has a job, people still need somewhere to live. That's my thinking, anyway. My uncle did that in the nineties and it's the reason he could stop working at fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get comfortable and don't do anything until year eight. I know myself. I'd need Chloe to keep nudging me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to get ready, so take it seriously but don't freak out. I'd say it to people on site and to my girlfriend's worried dad.
S4.think: Ten years means they'd probably be okay: he'd move into management, his girlfriend could retrain and they'd still marry. The end point bothers him, but he'd be 37 with savings and a plan.
S4.do: Keeps fitting and watching for a year, then takes a management course in year two or three. Puts savings into a small rental flat for income that doesn't depend on a job.
S4.feel: Uneasy, the kind that comes with knowing there's time.
S4.quote: My uncle did that in the nineties and it's the reason he could stop working at fifty.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Femi's plans include property as a hedge, inspired by his uncle. He knows he may coast too long and relies on his partner to push him. The household rather than the job is still his frame.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Chloe and I would both be hit before we'd done anything. What would help is decent income support while people retrain, and employers being told to give notice and pay for training before they bring the robots in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the nights. I've built forty shops in the dark that people walk into in daylight and never think about. If robots do it, I hope somebody at least turns the lights on.

headlineQuote: I've built forty shops in the dark that people walk into in daylight and never think about.
portrait: Femi Dubois is a 27-year-old shopfitter who works nights fitting out cafés and offices, owns his van outright and has about nine months of savings plus some work shares. He uses AI now and then for emails and translation and adopts new tools once he's seen them work. His main worry is the household: his girlfriend Chloe's insurance job looks more exposed than his. Calm in the mild pictures, he's alarmed by the two-year AGI picture and would delay engagement plans, while with more time he'd move into project management and buy a rental flat.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he and his girlfriend would both be hit before they'd had time to do anything.
whatWouldHelp: Decent income support while people retrain, and employers required to give notice and pay for training before bringing in robots.
